how to wire an LED
Wire GPIO -> 220 Ohm to 330 Ohm resistor -> LED anode, and LED cathode -> GND. Never connect an LED directly to a GPIO or supply rail without a resistor.

why use a resistor with LED

The resistor limits current. Without it, excess current flows through the LED and can burn it or the GPIO. Use R = (supply voltage - LED forward voltage) / target current, then check resistor power with P = I^2 * R.

calculate LED resistor

R = (Vsupply - Vforward) / I. For a red LED (Vf ~2V) at 15mA on a 5V board: R = (5 - 2) / 0.015 = 200 Ohm. Use a standard 220 Ohm resistor. Check power: P = 0.015^2 * 220 = 0.05W, well within 1/4W rating.

LED too dim

The resistor value may be too high, reducing current. Lower the resistance (e.g., from 1kOhm to 220 Ohm) but stay above the minimum safe value. Also verify supply voltage and LED forward voltage match your calculation.

ESP32 strapping pins (GPIO0, 2, 5, 12, 15) affect boot mode. Avoid connecting loads that pull them high or low during reset. If needed, use them only for outputs after boot completes.

what is ohm's law
Ohm's Law: V = I * R. Voltage (V) equals current (I) times resistance (R). Use it to calculate resistor values, current through components, and voltage drops. Also: P = V * I for power.

voltage divider
A voltage divider uses two resistors in series: Vout = Vin * R2 / (R1 + R2). Useful for reading 5V sensors on 3.3V boards, or scaling analog signals down to ADC range.

what is a pull-up resistor
A pull-up resistor connects a GPIO input to VCC (typically 4.7k-10k), ensuring a defined HIGH state when no other signal drives the pin. Used with buttons (to GND) and I2C lines.

what is a pull-down resistor
A pull-down resistor connects a GPIO input to GND (typically 4.7k-10k), ensuring a defined LOW state when no other signal drives the pin. Used when the active signal pulls HIGH.

floating input

A floating input is a GPIO set to INPUT but not connected to any defined voltage. It picks up random noise and reads unreliable values. Fix by adding a pull-up or pull-down resistor, or use INPUT_PULLUP.

what is pwm

PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) switches a pin rapidly between HIGH and LOW. The duty cycle controls the average voltage. Use it for LED dimming, motor speed control, and servo positioning. Not all pins support PWM.

what is i2c
I2C is a two-wire serial protocol using SDA (data) and SCL (clock). Multiple devices share the bus, each with a unique address. Needs pull-up resistors on both lines (usually 4.7k to VCC).

what is spi
SPI uses four wires: MOSI (data out), MISO (data in), SCK (clock), and CS (chip select per device). Faster than I2C but needs more pins. Used for displays, SD cards, and fast sensors.

UART is asynchronous serial communication using TX and RX at a set baud rate. Cross-connect TX to RX between devices. Common baud rates: 9600 (classic AVR), 115200 (modern boards).

3.3v vs 5v
Boards run at either 3.3V or 5V logic. Never connect a 5V output directly to a 3.3V GPIO — use a voltage divider or level shifter. Arduino Uno/Nano/Mega are 5V; ESP32, Pico, STM32, Teensy are 3.3V.

Level shifting converts signals between 3.3V and 5V logic. Options: bidirectional level-shifter modules (for I2C/SPI), voltage dividers (for unidirectional signals), or logic-level MOSFETs.
